summary: This informational RFC specifies two elliptic curves over prime fields, aimed at about 128-bit and 224-bit security levels, for use in cryptography including TLS. They are generated deterministically from a published list of requirements rather than from unexplained constants.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7748 specifies two elliptic curves, curve25519 and curve448, and functions for using them in cryptography. It also describes how to use the functions for Diffie-Hellman key agreement and how the curves were generated.

questions: how does x25519 key agreement work
subtitle: Two elliptic curves with specified key-agreement functions and a reproducible generation process.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic curve implementations need efficient operations and protection against side-channel leaks, while curve generation should be transparent.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies curve25519 and curve448, their X25519 and X448 functions, input and output formats, and a deterministic curve-generation procedure.
tldr.outcome: The curves support Diffie-Hellman key agreement. The RFC warns that large quantum computers would break both curves.

today: RFC 7748 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies curve25519, curve448, and the X25519 and X448 functions.

sections.title: Purpose and Design Goals
sections.content:
RFC 7748 specifies two elliptic curves over prime fields for cryptographic applications, including Transport Layer Security (TLS). They are intended for approximately 128-bit and 224-bit security levels.

The RFC says the curves support efficient implementation and a constant-time scalar multiplication method designed to resist side-channel attacks, including timing and cache attacks. It also explains how to use the curves for Diffie-Hellman key agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines two curves and the operations needed to use them in key agreement. Their design aims to make implementations efficient and reduce information leaks through timing or memory access.

sections.title: How the Curves Were Generated
sections.content:
Appendix A describes a deterministic procedure for choosing each curve's parameter from a prime field. The procedure aims to make the choices objective and reproducible, rather than relying on unexplained constants.

The requirements rule out specified trace values, require an embedding degree greater than (order - 1) / 100, and require a CM discriminant greater than 2^100. The appendix also explains how the cofactor and base point are selected and includes Sage scripts for generating the values.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors give a repeatable procedure for generating the curve parameters. It includes explicit mathematical checks and a procedure for selecting the base point.

sections.title: The Two Curves
sections.content:
Curve25519 uses the prime 2^255 - 19, has parameter A = 486662, cofactor 8, and base-point u-coordinate 9. Its intended security level is about 128 bits. The RFC also gives its equivalent twisted Edwards curve, edwards25519.

Curve448 uses the prime 2^448 - 2^224 - 1, has parameter A = 156326, cofactor 4, and base-point u-coordinate 5. Its intended security level is about 224 bits. The RFC gives its equivalent Edwards curves and their mappings as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Curve25519 and curve448 use different prime fields and have different security targets. The RFC specifies their parameters, base points, and related Edwards curves.

sections.title: The X25519 and X448 Functions
sections.content:
X25519 and X448 take a scalar and a u-coordinate and return a u-coordinate. Inputs and outputs are little-endian byte strings: 32 bytes for X25519 and 56 bytes for X448. X25519 implementations MUST mask the most significant bit of a received u-coordinate. Both functions MUST accept non-canonical values and process them as if reduced modulo the field prime.

The functions use a Montgomery ladder. Its conditional swap SHOULD be implemented in constant time. The RFC says that repeating the same sequence of field operations for every secret key avoids one common source of leakage, but memory access, jumps, and arithmetic must also avoid depending on secret bits.
sections.plainLanguage: X25519 and X448 turn a secret scalar and a curve coordinate into an output coordinate. The RFC specifies their byte formats and recommends implementing the conditional swap so its timing does not reveal the secret.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement
sections.content:
For X25519, each party generates 32 random bytes, applies the function to its scalar and the base-point coordinate 9, and sends the resulting public value to the other party. Each party then applies the function to its own scalar and the value received. Both obtain the same shared secret.

For X448, the corresponding inputs are 56 random bytes and base-point coordinate 5. The parties MAY check whether the shared result is all zero and abort if it is. The RFC says this result can occur when the other party supplies a point of small order. A key-derivation function can use the shared secret and both public values to derive a symmetric key.
sections.plainLanguage: Each party sends a public value made from its private scalar and the base point. Applying the function to the other party's value produces the same shared secret on both sides.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes curve25519 as slightly below the standard 128-bit security level and curve448 as approximately 224-bit. It says large quantum computers, if created, would break both curves.

Protocol designers must not assume that both parties' private keys always affect the shared key. An input point of small order can remove the other party's contribution, and checking for an all-zero result can detect this case. The RFC also warns that equivalent public keys exist and that using public keys as identifiers without including them in key derivation may create vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not assume that every input makes both parties' private keys affect the shared result. The RFC describes checks and key-derivation precautions, and warns that large quantum computers would break both curves.
